title: Predicting Crime: The Ethics of Algorithms in Criminal Justice
paras: Courts have always had to make predictions. A judge deciding whether to release a defendant on bail must estimate whether that person will return for trial or commit another offence in the meantime; a parole board must guess how a prisoner will behave once released. Traditionally, such judgements rested on experience and intuition. In a growing number of jurisdictions, however, they are now informed by statistical tools that convert factors such as age, criminal record and employment history into a numerical risk score. Supporters regard this as a long-overdue step towards rational decision-making. Critics fear that it risks automating injustice.

The case in favour begins with an uncomfortable truth about human judgement: it is noisy. Studies of sentencing have found that similar defendants can receive strikingly different outcomes depending on which judge hears the case, and even on the time of day or the decision-maker's mood. An algorithm, by contrast, applies the same formula every time, and its performance can be measured and audited. In some pilot schemes, the use of risk scores has been associated with a reduction in pre-trial detention without any increase in offending, suggesting that the tools can sometimes make the system both fairer and cheaper.

The most serious objection concerns the data on which such tools are trained. Historical records reflect policing patterns rather than offending itself. If officers patrol one neighbourhood far more intensively than another, more arrests will be recorded there, and residents will therefore appear riskier to the model, even if the underlying rates of wrongdoing are identical. The resulting scores may then justify still heavier patrols, creating a feedback loop in which the algorithm appears to confirm the very prejudice it has inherited. Arrest figures, in short, measure enforcement as much as behaviour.

Technical fixes are complicated by a deeper problem. Mathematicians have demonstrated that several intuitive definitions of fairness cannot all be satisfied simultaneously when groups have different recorded base rates of re-arrest. A tool can be equally accurate for two groups and yet wrongly label members of one group as dangerous more often than members of the other. Which kind of error matters more is not a technical question but a moral and political one, and it ought to be answered openly by legislators and the public, rather than quietly by software engineers.

A further difficulty is opacity. Many risk assessment tools are commercial products whose internal workings are protected as trade secrets. A defendant who is denied bail partly because of a score he cannot examine is, in effect, unable to challenge a piece of evidence used against him, which sits uneasily with the principle of due process. Defenders of the tools respond that judges are not fully transparent either. Yet a judge can be asked to give reasons and can be overturned on appeal; an unexplained number is far harder to contest.

The standard safeguard is to keep a human being in charge, with the score serving merely as advice. This is less reassuring than it sounds. Psychologists have documented automation bias, the tendency to defer to a numerical output, especially when the decision-maker is overworked or fears criticism for overriding it. Moreover, a label such as 'high risk' describes the proportion of people with a similar profile who reoffended, not what a particular individual will do. The apparent precision of a number can disguise how uncertain the underlying prediction really is.

It would be a mistake to demand either a complete ban or uncritical adoption. The fairest comparison is not between an algorithm and a flawless judge, but between an algorithm and the imperfect system that exists. Even so, certain conditions seem indispensable: independent validation before deployment, public disclosure of the methods used, the right of defendants to examine and contest their scores, and regular re-testing for discriminatory effects. A tool that cannot satisfy these requirements has no place in a courtroom, however accurate it claims to be.

title: Measuring Time: From Shadows to Atoms
paras: Time appears to be the most objective of quantities, flowing at the same rate for everyone, everywhere. Yet the history of how humans have measured it suggests something rather different. The hours, minutes and seconds that structure modern life are not natural facts but human constructions, shaped at each stage by the practical needs of the societies that devised them. To follow the development of the clock is therefore to follow changes in trade, religion, industry and government.

The earliest timekeepers relied on the sky. Ancient civilisations observed the shifting length and direction of shadows, and built sundials to divide the day into portions. These devices were useless at night and on cloudy days, so water clocks, in which liquid dripped at a roughly steady rate from one vessel to another, were developed as a supplement. Both systems usually divided daylight into twelve parts, which meant that an 'hour' in summer was considerably longer than an hour in winter. Such flexibility is hard for modern minds to accept, but it suited agricultural communities whose lives followed the sun.

The mechanical clock, which appeared in medieval Europe, changed this arrangement. Installed in monasteries and then in town towers, clocks sounded bells that coordinated prayer, markets and civic duties. Over time, equal hours, which did not vary by season, became the norm. Some historians argue that the public clock fostered a new discipline in which labour was measured by the hour and punctuality became a virtue. Others consider this claim exaggerated, pointing out that wage labour, factories and urban growth did at least as much to teach people to value time as the devices themselves.

Accuracy improved dramatically with the introduction of the pendulum in the seventeenth century, which reduced the typical error of a good clock from several minutes a day to a matter of seconds. The impetus was largely commercial and military. Sailors could calculate latitude from the stars, but finding longitude required knowing the exact time at a reference point, and an error of a few minutes could place a ship many kilometres from its true position. The development of a reliable marine chronometer, able to keep time despite the motion and temperature changes of a long voyage, thus had enormous economic value and saved many lives.

Even then, there was no single 'correct' time. Each town set its clocks by the local position of the sun, so noon in one city arrived minutes before noon in another a short distance to the west. This was tolerable when travel was slow. The arrival of railways made it chaotic, since timetables required shared hours across hundreds of kilometres. Companies adopted standard time for their own purposes, and many communities initially resisted, regarding the change as an outside interference with local custom. International agreement on time zones came later in the nineteenth century, a reminder that deciding what time it is has always been a political act as well as a scientific one.

The twentieth century brought a shift from mechanical to physical oscillations. Quartz crystals, which vibrate at a very stable frequency when an electric current passes through them, made cheap and accurate watches possible. Atomic clocks went further, using the regular radiation emitted by caesium atoms as their standard, and since the late 1960s the official second has been defined in precisely this way. Such devices are accurate to within a tiny fraction of a second over millions of years, and satellite navigation, financial trading and telecommunications networks depend on them. Paradoxically, the rotation of the Earth itself is slightly irregular, so occasional leap seconds are inserted into official time to keep it in step with the day.

Each stage in this story answered a specific social demand: farmers needed the seasons, merchants and navigators needed accuracy, railways needed uniformity, and digital networks need synchronisation. The lesson is that precision is never pursued for its own sake. As our instruments become ever more exact, it is worth remembering that the question of what time it is has been, and will remain, partly a matter of human agreement.

title: Antibiotic Resistance: Borrowed Time
paras: Few discoveries have saved as many lives as antibiotics. Routine surgery, cancer chemotherapy, organ transplants and the safe delivery of premature babies all depend on the ability to treat bacterial infections that would otherwise be fatal. It is therefore alarming that the effectiveness of these drugs is declining. Antibiotic resistance, the capacity of bacteria to survive medicines designed to kill them, is neither new nor unnatural; it is an inevitable consequence of evolution. What is new is the speed at which human behaviour has accelerated it.

The underlying mechanism is natural selection. When a population of bacteria is exposed to an antibiotic, susceptible individuals die, while any with a chance mutation that protects them survive and multiply. Their descendants then dominate the population. Complicating matters, bacteria can also exchange genes directly, even between different species, so that a resistance trait that arises in one organism can spread rapidly through an entire microbial community. Every course of antibiotics, however justified, therefore exerts selective pressure, and no use of these drugs is entirely free of cost.

Several practices have intensified the problem. Antibiotics are frequently prescribed for viral illnesses such as colds, against which they are powerless, often because patients expect treatment or because doctors cannot quickly confirm the cause. Patients sometimes stop taking a course once they feel better, leaving the hardiest bacteria alive. Agriculture is another major contributor: in many countries, healthy livestock receive antibiotics routinely, to prevent disease in crowded conditions or to promote growth. Hospitals, meanwhile, bring together large numbers of vulnerable patients and heavy drug use, creating ideal conditions for resistant strains to emerge and spread.

Public campaigns often place the blame on individual prescribers and patients, but this framing is contested. Doctors working under severe time pressure, without access to rapid diagnostic tests, may prescribe 'just in case'. In regions with poor sanitation, infections spread easily, which raises the demand for treatment in the first place. Moreover, in many low-income countries the greater problem is not overuse but lack of access: far more people die because they cannot obtain an effective antibiotic than because the drug has failed. Policies that restrict consumption without improving access could therefore do more harm than good.

A further difficulty lies in the development pipeline. Very few new classes of antibiotics have reached the market in recent decades. The reason is largely economic. A new antibiotic that works against resistant infections will, and should, be used sparingly and held in reserve, which means that its manufacturer sells little of it. Medicines for chronic conditions, taken daily for years, offer a far better return on investment, and several large companies have abandoned antibiotic research altogether. Some economists propose a subscription model, under which governments pay a fixed annual fee for access to a drug regardless of how much is used, thereby separating company revenue from sales volume.

Alternatives are being explored, though none is a complete substitute. Bacteriophages, viruses that attack bacteria, can be remarkably precise, but each must be matched to the particular bacterium causing an infection, which demands rapid diagnosis and extensive testing. Vaccines reduce infections and therefore the need for antibiotics; rapid diagnostic tools help doctors to distinguish bacterial from viral illness within minutes. Each of these measures is promising, yet they are most effective when deployed together with better hygiene and careful stewardship of existing drugs.

The most realistic conclusion is that resistance can be slowed but not abolished. No single remedy, whether a new drug, a stricter prescribing rule or a change in farming practice, will be sufficient. Progress requires a combination of measures: sensible use of existing medicines, investment in sanitation and vaccination, and financial reforms that make the search for new antibiotics worthwhile. Without them, humanity may find that it has been living on borrowed time, and that the era in which a simple infection was easily cured turns out to have been a brief interlude.
